results.summary: This is a factory test module designed to verify all I/O pins of the ASIC. It operates in three modes: mirroring the dedicated inputs to the outputs, mirroring the bidirectional pins to the outputs, or outputting an 8-bit counter on both the outputs and bidirectional pins. The mode is selected by the rst_n and sel pins. It requires no external hardware and is used during chip bring-up to confirm pin functionality.

This is a multi-use dot product accelerator that can compute vector dot products, minimums, and maximums of data lists. It is a 4-bit system that loads data via index and data pins and produces a 12-bit result after at least 16 clock cycles. It is intended to be used as a coprocessor driven by an RP2040 for vector calculations. The design was tested using Verilator simulation, focusing on numerical stability.

This design measures the frequency of an input signal and displays the result on a dual seven-segment display. It debounces the input, counts transitions over a configurable period, and divides the count by ten for display. The period can be set via input pins to match the clock frequency for accurate measurements. It requires a dual seven-segment PMOD and a frequency source, and includes a debug mode for monitoring internal state.

Goldcrest RISC-V is a microcoded RISC-V processor based on the SUBLEQ architecture. It interfaces with external SPI ROM and RAM, a UART, and GPIO pins, and supports three additional SPI devices. The design is intended to run at 20 MHz and requires external SPI memory chips and a UART connection. Testing has not yet been performed, so no silicon results are available.

This project implements grayscale conversion and Sobel filtering for edge detection in images. Pixels are sent via SPI, and the processing mode is selected through input pins, with options for bypass, grayscale, Sobel, or combined grayscale and Sobel. An internal LFSR can generate test pixels. The design requires an external SPI master, such as a Raspberry Pi, to send and receive data.

Minilogix is a configurable 8-bit input, 8-bit output logic block with optional internal feedback, intended to function like an FPGA logic element. It is loaded serially via dedicated pins and can be used for various logic functions once configuration software is available. Testing involves loading the logic block and applying digital inputs to verify the output. It requires only a way to set digital inputs and observe outputs.

This design implements a simple SPI-based 16-bit register file with magic cookie detection, a 16-bit sigma-delta modulator (1st or 2nd order), and a LUT-based sine generator. The modulator output can be filtered externally to produce analog voltages or sine waves. It is intended for testing the flow and requires external RC lowpass filters and monitoring equipment like a scope or voltmeter.

Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

This design is a multiplexer that allows selection of different IHP standard cells for testing. It uses page bits to select among cells and input bits to drive them, with outputs reflecting the selected cell's behavior. The documentation is minimal, with 'to be filled later' for how it works and how to test. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected, with manual testing of the mux and standard cells.

This is a latch test design that verifies the proper technology mapping of $_DLATCH_N_ and $_DLATCH_P_ cells. It provides a P latch and an N latch with enable and data inputs, and outputs to observe their behavior. The P latch is transparent when its enable is high, and the N latch when its enable is low. Silicon testing by both the author and an external tester confirmed correct operation.
